title: Authenticity and Writing With Artificial Intelligence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay argues that as AI-assisted writing becomes ubiquitous, readers will increasingly police the line between efficient communication and authentic, personally-authored expression. It concedes that AI can match a writer's voice and save enormous time on routine business documents, but contends that for symbolically loaded communication — condolence notes, personal letters, heartfelt advice — audiences who value authenticity will judge AI-generated messages as hollow or insincere. The piece predicts growing pressure on writers and artists to disclose whether AI assisted their work, and offers a simple gut-check: if you'd be embarrassed for someone to learn AI wrote a message, don't use AI to write it. It closes by noting that the newsletter itself deliberately avoids AI in its own writing and editing to preserve that authenticity.
points: Predicts a coming split between AI-tolerated communication (routine business writing) and AI-scrutinized communication (personal, symbolic messages).
Offers a practical litmus test: avoid AI whenever you'd feel embarrassed for others to learn it was used.
Frames authenticity as something that cannot be delegated to any intelligence other than one's own.
Anticipates that audiences will begin actively seeking out art, music, and writing that is explicitly human-made as AI proliferates.
Uses the newsletter's own no-AI editorial policy as a real-world example of the authenticity stance it's describing.
quotes: But readers of those words will become increasingly concerned with their authenticity. When others know an artificial intelligence is used to compose your words, readers will naturally question the sincerity, authenticity, and originality of that writing.

But more personal messages, such as blog posts, personal letters, heartfelt expressions, advice, and requests for assistance (among many other symbolic messages) will be scrutinized and treated harshly if and when AI is used to create them.
People will soon increasingly seek out music, art, novels, and other forms of creative expression that originate directly from artists and that do not use AI.
Field Notes does not rely on AI for writing or editing. By design and choice. The words, as imperfect as they are, come from real people with deep experience.
Here's a good rule: If you would feel embarrassed or awkward if others were to learn you used AI to create a message, then you should avoid using it.
